The name _Chicago_ is derived from a French rendering of the [indigenous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_languages_of_the_Americas "Indigenous languages of the Americas")[Miami–Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami%E2%80%93Illinois_language "Miami–Illinois language") word _šikaakwa_, which was a name for a wild relative of [onion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onion "Onion") and [garlic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garlic "Garlic") known to modern botanists as _[Allium tricoccum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allium\_tricoccum "Allium tricoccum")_.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-24)[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing\_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_] The first known reference to the site of the city of Chicago as "_Checagou_" was by [Robert de La Salle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9-Robert_Cavelier,_Sieur_de_La_Salle "René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle") around 1679 in a memoir.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-25)[Henri Joutel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Joutel "Henri Joutel"), in his journal of 1688, noted that the eponymous wild "garlic" grew profusely in the area.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-Swenson,_John_F._235%E2%80%93248-26) According to his diary of late September 1687:

> ... when we arrived at the said place called "Chicagou" which, according to what we were able to learn of it, has taken this name because of the quantity of garlic which grows in the forests in this region.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-Swenson,_John_F._235%E2%80%93248-26)

The city has had [several nicknames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicknames_of_Chicago "Nicknames of Chicago") throughout its history, such as the [Windy City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windy_City_(nickname) "Windy City (nickname)"), Chi-Town, Second City, and City of the Big Shoulders.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-Liebling's_Second_City-27)

## History

Main article: [History of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Chicago "History of Chicago")

For a chronological guide, see [Timeline of Chicago history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Chicago_history "Timeline of Chicago history").

### 18th century: Potawatomi, Jean Baptiste Point du Sable

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e6/Pottawatomi_Fashion_at_the_Field_Museum_in_Chicago.jpg/250px-Pottawatomi_Fashion_at_the_Field_Museum_in_Chicago.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pottawatomi_Fashion_at_the_Field_Museum_in_Chicago.jpg)

Traditional [Potawatomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potawatomi "Potawatomi") regalia on display at the [Field Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_Museum_of_Natural_History "Field Museum of Natural History")

In the mid-18th century, the area was inhabited by the [Potawatomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potawatomi "Potawatomi"), an indigenous tribe who had succeeded the [Miami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_people "Miami people"), [Sauk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sauk_people "Sauk people") and [Meskwaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meskwaki "Meskwaki") peoples in this region.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-28)

The first known permanent settler in Chicago was a trader, [Jean Baptiste Point du Sable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Baptiste_Point_du_Sable "Jean Baptiste Point du Sable"). Du Sable was of [African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_people "African people") descent, perhaps born in the [French colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_French_possessions_and_colonies "List of French possessions and colonies") of [Saint-Domingue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Domingue "Saint-Domingue") (Haiti), and he established the settlement in the 1780s. He is commonly known as the "Founder of Chicago".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGenzen200710%E2%80%9311,_14%E2%80%9315-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeating200530%E2%80%9331,_221-30)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-Swenson-31)

In 1795, following the victory of the new United States in the [Northwest Indian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Indian_War "Northwest Indian War"), an area that was to be part of Chicago was turned over to the U.S. for a military post by native tribes in accordance with the [Treaty of Greenville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Greenville "Treaty of Greenville").

### 19th century: Growth, major engineering projects

#### 1800–1849: Indian removal, first railroad and canal

In 1803, the [U.S. Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army") constructed [Fort Dearborn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Dearborn "Fort Dearborn"), which was destroyed during the [War of 1812](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_1812 "War of 1812") in the [Battle of Fort Dearborn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Fort_Dearborn "Battle of Fort Dearborn") by the Potawatomi before being later rebuilt.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGenzen200716%E2%80%9317-32)

The [Odawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa "Odawa"), [Ojibwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe "Ojibwe"), and Potawatomi tribes ceded additional land to the United States in the 1816 [Treaty of St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_St._Louis_(1816) "Treaty of St. Louis (1816)"). The Potawatomi were forcibly removed from their land after the [1833 Treaty of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1833_Treaty_of_Chicago "1833 Treaty of Chicago") and sent west of the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River") as part of the federal policy of [Indian removal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_removal "Indian removal").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBuisseret199022%E2%80%9323,_68,_80%E2%80%9381-33)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeating200530%E2%80%9332-34)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-Timeline:_Early_Chicago_History-35) On August 12, 1833, the Town of Chicago was organized with a population of about 200.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-Timeline:_Early_Chicago_History-35) Within seven years it grew to more than 6,000 people. On June 15, 1835, the first public land sales began with [Edmund Dick Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_Dick_Taylor "Edmund Dick Taylor") as Receiver of Public Monies. The City of Chicago was incorporated on Saturday, March 4, 1837,[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-36) and for several decades was the world's fastest-growing city.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-37)

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/Illinois-michigan-canal.png/250px-Illinois-michigan-canal.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Illinois-michigan-canal.png)

The location and course of the [Illinois and Michigan Canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_and_Michigan_Canal "Illinois and Michigan Canal") (completed 1848)

[Video 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/95/Corner_Madison_and_State_streets%2C_Chicago_-.webm?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)

[State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Street_(Chicago) "State Street (Chicago)") and [Madison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_Street_(Chicago) "Madison Street (Chicago)") streets, once known as the busiest intersection in the world (1897)

As the site of the [Chicago Portage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Portage "Chicago Portage"),[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeating200527-38) the city became an important transportation hub between the eastern and western United States. Chicago's first railway, [Galena and Chicago Union Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galena_and_Chicago_Union_Railroad "Galena and Chicago Union Railroad"), and the [Illinois and Michigan Canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_and_Michigan_Canal "Illinois and Michigan Canal") opened in 1848. The canal allowed [steamboats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steamboat "Steamboat") and [sailing ships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sailing_ship "Sailing ship") on the [Great Lakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes "Great Lakes") to connect to the Mississippi River.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBuisseret199086%E2%80%9398-39)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTECondit197330%E2%80%9331-40)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGenzen200724%E2%80%9325-41)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeating200526%E2%80%9329,_35%E2%80%9339-42)

A flourishing economy brought residents from rural communities and [immigrants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immigration_to_the_United_States "Immigration to the United States") from abroad. Manufacturing and retail and finance sectors became dominant, influencing the [American economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_economy "American economy").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-43) The [Chicago Board of Trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Board_of_Trade "Chicago Board of Trade") (established 1848) listed the first-ever standardized "exchange-traded" forward contracts, which were called [futures contracts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Futures_contract "Futures contract").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-44)

#### 1850–1874: Raising, water cribs, river reversal, fire

In the 1850s, Chicago gained national political prominence as the home of Senator [Stephen Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Douglas "Stephen Douglas"), the champion of the [Kansas–Nebraska Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas%E2%80%93Nebraska_Act "Kansas–Nebraska Act") and the "popular sovereignty" approach to the issue of the spread of slavery.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-45) These issues also helped propel another Illinoisan, [Abraham Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln "Abraham Lincoln"), to the national stage. Lincoln was nominated in Chicago for U.S. president at the [1860 Republican National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1860_Republican_National_Convention "1860 Republican National Convention"), which was held in a purpose-built auditorium called the [Wigwam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wigwam_(Chicago) "Wigwam (Chicago)"). He defeated Douglas in the general election, and this set the stage for the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War").

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4b/Cook_County_Court_House_and_City_Hall_1855.jpg/250px-Cook_County_Court_House_and_City_Hall_1855.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cook_County_Court_House_and_City_Hall_1855.jpg)

1855 [daguerreotype](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daguerreotype "Daguerreotype") attributed to [Alexander Hesler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Hesler "Alexander Hesler") of the Cook County Court House and City Hall. Believed to be the oldest surviving photograph taken of a structure in Chicago.

To accommodate rapid population growth and demand for better sanitation, the city improved its infrastructure. In February 1856, Chicago's Common Council approved [Chesbrough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellis_S._Chesbrough "Ellis S. Chesbrough")'s plan to build the United States' first comprehensive sewerage system.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-46) The project [raised much of central Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raising_of_Chicago "Raising of Chicago") to a new grade with the use of [jackscrews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackscrews "Jackscrews") for raising buildings.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-47) While elevating Chicago, and at first improving the city's health, the untreated sewage and industrial waste now flowed into the [Chicago River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_River "Chicago River"), and subsequently into [Lake Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Michigan "Lake Michigan"), polluting the city's primary freshwater source.

The city responded by tunneling two miles (3.2 km) out into Lake Michigan to newly built [water cribs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_cribs_in_Chicago "Water cribs in Chicago"). In 1900, the problem of sewage contamination was largely resolved when the city completed a major engineering feat. It reversed the flow of the Chicago River so that the water flowed away from Lake Michigan rather than into it. This project began with the construction and improvement of the Illinois and Michigan Canal, and was completed with the [Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Sanitary_and_Ship_Canal "Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal") that connects to the [Illinois River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_River "Illinois River"), which flows into the Mississippi River.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTECondit197315%E2%80%9318,_243%E2%80%93245-48)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGenzen200727%E2%80%9329,_38%E2%80%9343-49)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBuisseret1990154%E2%80%93155,_172%E2%80%93173,_204%E2%80%93205-50)

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Chicago_in_Flames_by_Currier_%26_Ives%2C_1871_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Chicago_in_Flames_by_Currier_%26_Ives%2C_1871_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chicago_in_Flames_by_Currier_&_Ives,_1871_(cropped).jpg)

Illustration of the [Great Chicago Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire "Great Chicago Fire")

On October 8, 1871, the [Great Chicago Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire "Great Chicago Fire") destroyed an area about 4 miles (6.4 km) long and 1-mile (1.6 km) wide, a large section of the city at the time. At least 300 people were killed and over 100,000 were left homeless from the fire.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBuisseret1990148%E2%80%93149-51)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGenzen200732%E2%80%9337-52)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTELowe200087%E2%80%9397-53) However, much of the city, including [railroads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railroads "Railroads") and [stockyards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Stock_Yard "Union Stock Yard"), survived intact,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTELowe200099-54) and from the ruins of the previous wooden structures arose more modern constructions of steel and stone. These set a precedent worldwide for construction.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-55)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTECondit19739%E2%80%9311-56) During its rebuilding period, Chicago constructed the world's [first skyscraper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Insurance_Building "Home Insurance Building") in 1885, using [steel-skeleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steel_frame "Steel frame") construction.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-57)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTELowe2000121,_129-58)

#### 1875–1899: Railroads, annexation, health, stature

[Labor conflicts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_history_of_the_United_States "Labor history of the United States") followed the industrial boom and the rapid expansion of the labor pool during the [Gilded Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilded_Age "Gilded Age"), including the [Haymarket affair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haymarket_affair "Haymarket affair") on May 4, 1886, and in 1894 the [Pullman Strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pullman_Strike "Pullman Strike"). [Anarchist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anarchism "Anarchism") and socialist groups played prominent roles in creating very large and highly organized labor actions. Concern for social problems among Chicago's immigrant poor led [Jane Addams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Addams "Jane Addams") and [Ellen Gates Starr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellen_Gates_Starr "Ellen Gates Starr") to found [Hull House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hull_House "Hull House") in 1889.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-59) Programs that were developed there became a model for the new field of [social work](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_work "Social work").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-hullhouse-60)

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/Home_Insurance_Building.JPG/250px-Home_Insurance_Building.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Home_Insurance_Building.JPG)

[Home Insurance Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Insurance_Building "Home Insurance Building") (1885)

During the 1870s and 1880s, Chicago attained national stature as the leader in the movement to improve public health. City laws and later, state laws that upgraded standards for the medical profession and fought urban epidemics of [cholera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cholera "Cholera"), [smallpox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smallpox "Smallpox"), and [yellow fever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever "Yellow fever") were both passed and enforced. These laws became templates for public health reform in other cities and states.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-61)

The city established many large, well-landscaped [municipal parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Park_District "Chicago Park District"), which also included public sanitation facilities. The chief advocate for improving public health in Chicago was [John H. Rauch, M.D.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Henry_Rauch "John Henry Rauch") Rauch established a plan for Chicago's park system in 1866. He created [Lincoln Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_Park "Lincoln Park") by closing a cemetery filled with shallow graves, and in 1867, in response to an outbreak of cholera he helped establish a new Chicago Board of Health. Ten years later, he became the secretary and then the president of the first Illinois State Board of Health, which carried out most of its activities in Chicago.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-62)

In the 1800s, Chicago became the nation's railroad hub, and by 1910 over 20 railroads operated passenger service out of six different downtown terminals.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTECondit197343%E2%80%9349,_58,_318%E2%80%93319-63)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-64) In 1883, Chicago's railway managers needed a general time convention, so they developed the standardized system of North American [time zones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_zone "Time zone").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-65) This system for telling time spread throughout the continent.

The city grew significantly in size and population by incorporating many neighboring townships between 1851 and 1920, with the largest annexation happening in 1889, with five townships joining the city, including the [Hyde Park Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyde_Park_Township,_Cook_County,_Illinois "Hyde Park Township, Cook County, Illinois"), which now comprises most of the [South Side of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Side_of_Chicago "South Side of Chicago") and the far southeast of Chicago, and the [Jefferson Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_Township,_Cook_County,_Illinois "Jefferson Township, Cook County, Illinois"), which now makes up most of [Chicago's Northwest Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Side,_Chicago "Northwest Side, Chicago").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-66) The desire to join the city was driven by municipal services that the city could provide its residents.

[![Image 28](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/Looking_West_From_Peristyle%2C_Court_of_Honor_and_Grand_Basin%2C_1893.jpg/250px-Looking_West_From_Peristyle%2C_Court_of_Honor_and_Grand_Basin%2C_1893.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Looking_West_From_Peristyle,_Court_of_Honor_and_Grand_Basin,_1893.jpg)

Court of Honor at the [World's Columbian Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_Columbian_Exposition "World's Columbian Exposition") in 1893

In 1893, Chicago hosted the [World's Columbian Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_Columbian_Exposition "World's Columbian Exposition") on former marshland at the present location of [Jackson Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_Park_(Chicago) "Jackson Park (Chicago)"). The Exposition drew 27.5 million visitors, and is considered the most influential [world's fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_fair "World's fair") in history.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-67)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTELowe2000148%E2%80%93154,_158%E2%80%93169-68) The city's municipal device, a Y within a circle, was the result of a contest run by the _Chicago Tribune_ in 1892, in anticipation of the Columbian Exposition.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-69) The [University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago"), formerly at another location, moved to the same South Side location in 1892. The term "midway" for a fair or carnival referred originally to the [Midway Plaisance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midway_Plaisance "Midway Plaisance"), a strip of park land that still runs through the University of Chicago campus and connects the [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Park_(Chicago_park) "Washington Park (Chicago park)") and Jackson Parks.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-70)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-71)

### 20th century: More growth, pluralization, suburbs, Daleys

#### 1900–1924: Industrial growth, prohibition

[Video 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d4/Chicago_Photographed_from_Ray_Knabenshue%27s_Dirigible_Air_Ship.webm?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)

Aerial motion film photography of Chicago in 1914 as filmed by [A. Roy Knabenshue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._Roy_Knabenshue "A. Roy Knabenshue")

Chicago's flourishing economy attracted huge numbers of new immigrants from [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe") and migrants from the [Eastern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_United_States "Eastern United States"). Of the total population in 1900, more than 77% were either foreign-born or born in the United States of foreign parentage. [Germans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germans "Germans"), [Irish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_people "Irish people"), [Poles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_people "Polish people"), [Swedes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedes "Swedes"), and [Czechs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czechs "Czechs") made up nearly two-thirds of the foreign-born population (by 1900, whites were 98.1% of the city's population).[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-72)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-73)

During [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") and the 1920s there was a major expansion in industry. The availability of jobs attracted African Americans from the [Southern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_United_States "Southern United States"). Between 1910 and 1930, the African American population of Chicago increased dramatically, from 44,103 to 233,903.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-74) This [Great Migration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Migration_(African_American) "Great Migration (African American)") had an immense cultural impact, called the [Chicago Black Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Black_Renaissance "Chicago Black Renaissance"), part of the [New Negro Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Negro_Movement "New Negro Movement"), in art, literature, and music.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-75) Continuing racial tensions and violence in the city, such as the [Chicago race riot of 1919](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_race_riot_of_1919 "Chicago race riot of 1919"), also occurred.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-76)

The ratification of the 18th amendment to the Constitution in 1919 made the production and sale (including exportation) of alcoholic beverages illegal in the United States. This ushered in the beginning of what is known as the gangster era, a time that roughly spans from 1919 until 1933 when [Prohibition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prohibition_in_the_United_States "Prohibition in the United States") was repealed. The 1920s saw [gangsters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_gangsters_during_the_1920s "American gangsters during the 1920s"), including [Al Capone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Capone "Al Capone"), [Dion O'Banion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dion_O'Banion "Dion O'Banion"), [Bugs Moran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bugs_Moran "Bugs Moran") and [Tony Accardo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Accardo "Tony Accardo") battle law enforcement and each other on the streets of Chicago during the Prohibition era.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-77) Chicago was the location of the infamous [St. Valentine's Day Massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Valentine's_Day_Massacre "St. Valentine's Day Massacre") in 1929, when Al Capone sent men to gun down members of a rival gang, North Side, led by Bugs Moran, leaving seven rival members dead.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-78)

[![Image 29](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/83/Breaking_the_Landlords%27_Lease_on_Peace.jpg/250px-Breaking_the_Landlords%27_Lease_on_Peace.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Breaking_the_Landlords'_Lease_on_Peace.jpg)

Chicago tenants picket against rent increases (March 1920)

From 1920 to 1921, [the city was affected by a series of tenant rent strikes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1920%E2%80%931921_Chicago_rent_strikes "1920–1921 Chicago rent strikes"), which led to the formation of the Chicago Tenants Protective association, passage of the Kessenger tenant laws, and of a heat ordinance that legally required flats to be kept above 68°F during winter months by landlords.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-79)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-80)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-81)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-82)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-83)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-84)

Chicago was the first American city to have a homosexual-rights organization. The organization, formed in 1924, was called the [Society for Human Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_for_Human_Rights "Society for Human Rights"). It produced the first American publication for homosexuals, _[Friendship and Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friendship\_and\_Freedom "Friendship and Freedom")_. Police and political pressure caused the organization to disband.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-85)

Men outside a soup kitchen during the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression") (1931)

#### 1925–1949: Great Depression, Great Migration

The Great Depression brought unprecedented suffering to Chicago, in no small part due to the city's heavy reliance on heavy industry. Notably, industrial areas on the south side and neighborhoods lining both branches of the Chicago River were devastated; by 1933 over 50% of industrial jobs in the city had been lost, and unemployment rates amongst blacks and Latinos in the city were over 40%. The Republican political machine in Chicago was utterly destroyed by the economic crisis, and every mayor since 1931 has been a [Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)").[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-Great_Depression-86)

From 1928 to 1933, the city witnessed a tax revolt, and the city was unable to meet payroll or provide relief efforts. The fiscal crisis was resolved by 1933, and at the same time, federal relief funding began to flow into Chicago.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-Great_Depression-86) Chicago was also a hotbed of labor activism, with [Unemployed Councils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unemployed_Councils "Unemployed Councils") contributing heavily in the early depression to create solidarity for the poor and demand relief; these organizations were created by socialist and communist groups. By 1935, the [Workers Alliance of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Workers_Alliance_of_America "Workers Alliance of America") began organizing the poor, workers, the unemployed. In the spring of 1937 Republic Steel Works witnessed the [Memorial Day massacre of 1937](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Day_massacre_of_1937 "Memorial Day massacre of 1937") in the neighborhood of East Side.

In 1933, Chicago Mayor [Anton Cermak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anton_Cermak "Anton Cermak") was fatally wounded in [Miami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami "Miami"), Florida, during a [failed assassination attempt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attempted_assassination_of_Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Attempted assassination of Franklin D. Roosevelt") on President-elect [Franklin D. Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Franklin D. Roosevelt") by [Giuseppe Zangara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Zangara "Giuseppe Zangara"). In 1933 and 1934, the city celebrated its centennial by hosting the [Century of Progress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Century_of_Progress "Century of Progress") International Exposition [World's Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_Fair "World's Fair").[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-87) The theme of the fair was technological innovation over the century since Chicago's founding.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-88)

[![Image 31](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/05/2004-09-07_1800x2400_chicago_picasso.jpg/250px-2004-09-07_1800x2400_chicago_picasso.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2004-09-07_1800x2400_chicago_picasso.jpg)

The [Chicago Picasso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Picasso "Chicago Picasso") (1967) inspired a new era in urban public art.

During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), the city of Chicago alone produced more steel than the United Kingdom every year from 1939 – 1945, and more than [Nazi Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany") from 1943 – 1945.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-89)

[![Image 32](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/1968_Democratic_National_Convention%2C_Chicago._Sept_68_C15_8_1313%2C_Photo_by_Bea_A_Corson%2C_Chicago._Purchased_at_estate_sale_in_2011_by_Victor_Grigas_Released_Public_Domain.tiff/lossy-page1-250px-thumbnail.tiff.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1968_Democratic_National_Convention,_Chicago._Sept_68_C15_8_1313,_Photo_by_Bea_A_Corson,_Chicago._Purchased_at_estate_sale_in_2011_by_Victor_Grigas_Released_Public_Domain.tiff)

Protesters in [Grant Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant_Park_(Chicago) "Grant Park (Chicago)") outside the [1968 Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_Democratic_National_Convention "1968 Democratic National Convention")

The Great Migration, which had been on pause due to the Depression, resumed at an even faster pace in the [second wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Great_Migration_(African_American) "Second Great Migration (African American)"), as hundreds of thousands of blacks from the South arrived in the city to work in the steel mills, railroads, and shipping yards.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-90)

On December 2, 1942, physicist [Enrico Fermi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrico_Fermi "Enrico Fermi") conducted the world's first controlled [nuclear reaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Pile-1 "Chicago Pile-1") at the University of Chicago as part of the top-secret [Manhattan Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_Project "Manhattan Project"). This led to the creation of the atomic bomb by the United States, which it used in [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") in 1945.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-91)

#### 1950–1974: Suburbanization, Richard J. Daley

Mayor [Richard J. Daley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_J._Daley "Richard J. Daley"), a Democrat, was elected in 1955, in the era of [machine politics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_machine "Political machine"). In 1956, the city conducted its last major expansion when it annexed the land under O'Hare airport, including a small portion of DuPage County.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-92)

By the 1960s, white residents in several neighborhoods left the city for the suburban areas – in many American cities, a process known as [white flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_flight "White flight") – as Blacks continued to move beyond the [Black Belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Belt_(region_of_Chicago) "Black Belt (region of Chicago)").[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-93) While home loan discriminatory [redlining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redlining "Redlining") against blacks continued, the real estate industry practiced what became known as [blockbusting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockbusting "Blockbusting"), completely changing the racial composition of whole neighborhoods.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-Mehlhorn-94) Structural changes in industry, such as globalization and job outsourcing, caused heavy job losses for lower-skilled workers. At its peak during the 1960s, some 250,000 workers were employed in the steel industry in Chicago, but the steel crisis of the 1970s and 1980s reduced this number to just 28,000 in 2015. In 1966, [Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Martin Luther King Jr.") and [Albert Raby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Raby "Albert Raby") led the [Chicago Freedom Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Freedom_Movement "Chicago Freedom Movement"), which culminated in agreements between Mayor Richard J. Daley and the movement leaders.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-95)

Two years later, the city hosted the tumultuous [1968 Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_Democratic_National_Convention "1968 Democratic National Convention"), which featured physical confrontations both inside and outside the convention hall, with anti-war protesters, journalists and bystanders being beaten by police.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-96) Major construction projects, including the Sears Tower (now known as the [Willis Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willis_Tower "Willis Tower"), which in 1974 became the [world's tallest building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tallest_buildings_and_structures_in_the_world "List of tallest buildings and structures in the world")), [University of Illinois at Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Chicago "University of Illinois at Chicago"), [McCormick Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCormick_Place "McCormick Place"), and [O'Hare International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O'Hare_International_Airport "O'Hare International Airport"), were undertaken during Richard J. Daley's tenure.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-97)

#### 1975–1999: Decline, diversity, Richard M. Daley

In 1979, [Jane Byrne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Byrne "Jane Byrne"), the city's first female mayor, was elected. She was notable for temporarily moving into the crime-ridden [Cabrini-Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabrini-Green "Cabrini-Green") housing project and leading Chicago's school system out of a financial crisis.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-98)

In 1983, [Harold Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Washington "Harold Washington") became the first black mayor of Chicago. Washington's first term in office directed attention to poor and previously neglected minority neighborhoods. He was re‑elected in 1987 but died of a heart attack soon after.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-99) Washington was succeeded by 6th ward alderperson [Eugene Sawyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_Sawyer "Eugene Sawyer"), who was elected by the Chicago City Council and served until a special election.

[Richard M. Daley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_M._Daley "Richard M. Daley"), son of Richard J. Daley, was elected in 1989. His accomplishments included improvements to parks and creating incentives for [sustainable development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sustainable_development "Sustainable development"), as well as closing [Meigs Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meigs_Field "Meigs Field") in the middle of the night and destroying the runways. After successfully running for re-election five times, and becoming Chicago's longest-serving mayor, Richard M. Daley declined to run for a seventh term.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-100)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-101)

In 1992, a construction accident near the [Kinzie Street Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinzie_Street_Bridge "Kinzie Street Bridge") produced a breach connecting the Chicago River to a tunnel below, which was part of an [abandoned freight tunnel system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Tunnel_Company "Chicago Tunnel Company") extending throughout the downtown [Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Loop "Chicago Loop") district. The [tunnels filled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_flood "Chicago flood") with 250 million US gallons (1,000,000 m 3) of water, affecting buildings throughout the district and forcing a shutdown of electrical power.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-CBS2-102) The area was shut down for three days and some buildings did not reopen for weeks; losses were estimated at $1.95 billion.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-CBS2-102)

### 21st century

#### 2000–2025: Deficits, diverse city government

On February 23, 2011, [Rahm Emanuel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rahm_Emanuel "Rahm Emanuel"), a former [White House Chief of Staff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House_Chief_of_Staff "White House Chief of Staff") and member of the [House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives"), won the mayoral election.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-103) Emanuel was sworn in as mayor on May 16, 2011, and won re-election in 2015.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-104)[Lori Lightfoot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lori_Lightfoot "Lori Lightfoot"), the city's first African American woman mayor and its first openly LGBTQ mayor, was elected to succeed Emanuel as mayor in 2019.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-105) All three city-wide elective offices were held by women (and women of color) for the first time in Chicago history: in addition to Lightfoot, the city clerk was [Anna Valencia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_M._Valencia "Anna M. Valencia") and the city treasurer was [Melissa Conyears-Ervin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melissa_Conyears "Melissa Conyears").[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-106)On May 15, 2023, [Brandon Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandon_Johnson "Brandon Johnson") assumed office as the 57th mayor of Chicago.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-cbsnews-mayor-107)

In the 2020s, the city entered a fiscal crisis, the result of decades of underfunded municipal pensions. The city's budget deficit neared $1 billion in 2025.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-108)[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-109) The crisis occurred against the backdrop of a statewide budget crisis.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-110)

### Topography

[![Image 34](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Chicago-00.jpg/250px-Chicago-00.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chicago-00.jpg)

[![Image 36](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Chicago_by_Sentinel-2.jpg/250px-Chicago_by_Sentinel-2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chicago_by_Sentinel-2.jpg)

A satellite image of Chicago

Chicago is located in northeastern Illinois on the southwestern shores of freshwater Lake Michigan. It is the principal city in the [Chicago Metropolitan Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Metropolitan_Area "Chicago Metropolitan Area"), situated in both the [Midwestern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midwestern_United_States "Midwestern United States") and the [Great Lakes region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes_region_(North_America) "Great Lakes region (North America)"). The city rests on a [continental divide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_divide "Continental divide") at the site of the Chicago Portage, connecting the Mississippi River and the Great Lakes [watersheds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drainage_basin "Drainage basin"). In addition to it lying beside Lake Michigan, two rivers—the Chicago River in downtown and the [Calumet River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calumet_River "Calumet River") in the industrial far South Side—flow either entirely or partially through the city.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTECondit19735%E2%80%936-111)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGenzen20076%E2%80%939-112)

Chicago's history and economy are closely tied to its proximity to Lake Michigan. While the Chicago River historically handled much of the region's waterborne cargo, today's huge [lake freighters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_freighter "Lake freighter") use the city's [Lake Calumet Harbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_of_Chicago "Port of Chicago") on the South Side. The lake also provides another positive effect: moderating Chicago's climate, making waterfront neighborhoods slightly warmer in winter and cooler in summer.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-113)

When Chicago was founded in 1837, most of the early building was around the mouth of the Chicago River, as can be seen on a map of the city's original 58 blocks.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-114) The overall [grade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_grading "Land grading") of the city's central, built-up areas is relatively consistent with the natural flatness of its overall natural geography, generally exhibiting only slight differentiation otherwise. The average land elevation is 579 ft (176.5 m)[above sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Above_mean_sea_level "Above mean sea level"). While measurements vary somewhat,[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-115) the lowest points are along the lake shore at 578 ft (176.2 m), while the highest point, at 672 ft (205 m), is the morainal ridge of [Blue Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly,_Chicago "Beverly, Chicago") in the city's far south side.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-neiu-116)

[Lake Shore Drive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Shore_Drive "Lake Shore Drive") runs adjacent to a large portion of Chicago's waterfront. Some of the parks along the waterfront include [Lincoln Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_Park "Lincoln Park"), [Grant Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant_Park_(Chicago) "Grant Park (Chicago)"), [Burnham Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burnham_Park_(Chicago) "Burnham Park (Chicago)"), and [Jackson Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_Park_(Chicago) "Jackson Park (Chicago)"). There are 24 public [beaches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_beaches "Chicago beaches") across 26 miles (42 km) of the waterfront.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-usabeaches-117) Landfill extends into portions of the lake providing space for [Navy Pier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navy_Pier "Navy Pier"), [Northerly Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northerly_Island "Northerly Island"), the [Museum Campus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_Campus_Chicago "Museum Campus Chicago"), and large portions of the [McCormick Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCormick_Place "McCormick Place") Convention Center. Most of the city's high-rise commercial and residential buildings are close to the waterfront.

An informal name for the entire [Chicago metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_metropolitan_area "Chicago metropolitan area") is "Chicagoland", which generally means the city and all its suburbs, though different organizations have slightly different definitions.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-118)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-119)[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-120)

Major sections of the city include the central business district, called [the Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Loop "Chicago Loop"), and the North, [South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Side,_Chicago "South Side, Chicago"), and [West Sides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Side,_Chicago "West Side, Chicago").[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-121) The three sides of the city are represented on the [Flag of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_of_Chicago "Flag of Chicago") by three horizontal white stripes.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-122) The North Side is the city's most densely populated residential section, and many high-rises are on this side of the city along the lakefront.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-123) The South Side is the city's largest section, encompassing roughly 60% of its land area. The South Side contains most of the facilities of the [Port of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_of_Chicago "Port of Chicago").[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-124)

In the late 1920s, sociologists at the University of Chicago subdivided the city into 75 distinct [community areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_areas_in_Chicago "Community areas in Chicago"), plus O'Hare in 1956 and Edgewater in 1980 for a total of 77. The community areas can further be subdivided into over 200 informally defined [neighborhoods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neighborhoods_in_Chicago "Neighborhoods in Chicago").[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-125)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-126)

### Streetscape

Main article: [Roads and expressways in Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roads_and_expressways_in_Chicago "Roads and expressways in Chicago")

Chicago's streets were laid out in a [street grid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grid_plan "Grid plan") that grew from the city's original townsite plot, which was bounded by Lake Michigan on the east, North Avenue on the north, Wood Street on the west, and 22nd Street on the south.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-127) Streets following the [Public Land Survey System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Land_Survey_System "Public Land Survey System") section lines later became arterial streets in outlying sections. As new additions to the city were platted, city ordinance required them to be laid out with eight streets to the mile in one direction and sixteen in the other direction, about one street per 200 meters in one direction and one street per 100 meters in the other direction. The grid's regularity provided an efficient means of developing new real estate property. A scattering of diagonal streets, many of them originally Native American trails, also cross the city (Elston, Milwaukee, Ogden, Lincoln, etc.). Many additional diagonal streets were recommended in the [Plan of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burnham_Plan "Burnham Plan"), but only the extension of [Ogden Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ogden_Avenue_(Chicago) "Ogden Avenue (Chicago)") was ever constructed.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTECondit197331,_52%E2%80%9353-128)

In 2021, Chicago was ranked the fourth-most walkable large city in the United States.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-129) Many of the city's residential streets have a wide patch of grass or trees between the street and the sidewalk itself. This helps to keep pedestrians on the sidewalk further away from the street traffic. Chicago's [Western Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Avenue_(Chicago) "Western Avenue (Chicago)") is the longest continuous urban street in the world.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-El-KhouryRobbins2004-130) Other notable streets include [Michigan Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Avenue_(Chicago) "Michigan Avenue (Chicago)"), [State Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Street_(Chicago) "State Street (Chicago)"), [95th Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/95th_Street_(Chicago) "95th Street (Chicago)"), [Cicero Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicero_Avenue "Cicero Avenue"), [Clark Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Street_(Chicago) "Clark Street (Chicago)"), and [Belmont Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Avenue_(Chicago) "Belmont Avenue (Chicago)"). The destruction caused by the Great Chicago Fire led to the largest building boom in the history of the nation. Atwood, John Root, and [Helmut Jahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Jahn "Helmut Jahn").[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBach1980[httpsarchiveorgdetailschicagosfamousbu00condpagen60_9]-135)[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-FOOTNOTELowe2000118%E2%80%93127-136)

Chicago gave its name to the Chicago School and was home to the [Prairie School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prairie_School "Prairie School"), two movements in architecture.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago#cite_note-139) Multiple kinds and scales of houses, townhouses, condominiums, and apartment buildings can be found throughout Chicago. **Los Angeles** (often shortened as **LA** or **L.A.**)[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-16) is the [most populous city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_California "List of municipalities in California") in the U.S. state of [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), and the commercial, [financial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_District,_Los_Angeles "Financial District, Los Angeles"), and [cultural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_Los_Angeles "Culture of Los Angeles") center of [Southern California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_California "Southern California"). With an estimated 3.87 million residents within the city limits as of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Los_Angeles&action=edit),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-QuickFacts-8) it is the [second-most populous city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_cities_by_population "List of United States cities by population") in the United States, behind [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), and the largest city in the [Western United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_United_States "Western United States"). The city has an [ethnically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnic_groups_in_Los_Angeles "Ethnic groups in Los Angeles") and culturally diverse population, and is the principal city of a [metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_statistical_areas "Metropolitan statistical areas") of 12.9 million people (2024). [Greater Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Los_Angeles "Greater Los Angeles"), a [combined statistical area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combined_statistical_area "Combined statistical area") that includes the Los Angeles and [Riverside–San Bernardino metropolitan areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inland_Empire "Inland Empire"), is a sprawling [metropolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolis "Metropolis") of over 18 million residents.

The majority of the city proper lies in the [Los Angeles Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Basin "Los Angeles Basin") adjacent to the Pacific Ocean in the west and extending partly through the [Santa Monica Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Monica_Mountains "Santa Monica Mountains") and north into the [San Fernando Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Fernando_Valley "San Fernando Valley"), with the city bordering the [San Gabriel Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Gabriel_Valley "San Gabriel Valley") to its east. It covers about 469 square miles (1,210 km 2),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-CenPopGazetteer2021-6) and is the [county seat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_seat "County seat") and most populated city of [Los Angeles County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_County,_California "Los Angeles County, California"), which is the [most populous county in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_the_most_populous_counties_in_the_United_States "List of the most populous counties in the United States") with an estimated 9.86 million residents as of 2022[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Los_Angeles&action=edit).[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-LosAngelesCountyDecline2022-17) It is the [third-most visited city in the U.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_the_United_States "Tourism in the United States") (after New York City and [Miami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami "Miami")), with over 3.6 million visitors as of 2023.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-18)

The area that became Los Angeles was originally inhabited by the [indigenous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_people_of_California "Indigenous people of California")[Tongva people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tongva "Tongva") and later claimed by [Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Rodr%C3%ADguez_Cabrillo "Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo") for [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire") in 1542. The city was founded on September 4, 1781, under Spanish governor [Felipe de Neve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felipe_de_Neve "Felipe de Neve"), on the village of [Yaanga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yaanga "Yaanga").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-:02-19) It became a part of the [First Mexican Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Mexican_Empire "First Mexican Empire") in 1821 following the [Mexican War of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican_War_of_Independence "Mexican War of Independence"). In 1848, at the end of the [Mexican–American War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican%E2%80%93American_War "Mexican–American War"), Los Angeles and the rest of California were purchased as part of the [Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Guadalupe_Hidalgo "Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo") and became part of the United States. Los Angeles was [incorporated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipal_corporation "Municipal corporation") as a municipality on April 4, 1850, five months before California achieved [statehood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state"). The discovery of [oil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petroleum "Petroleum") in the 1890s brought rapid growth to the city.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-20) The city was further expanded with the completion of the [Los Angeles Aqueduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Aqueduct "Los Angeles Aqueduct") in 1913, which delivers water from [Eastern California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_California "Eastern California").

Los Angeles has a diverse economy with a broad range of industries. Despite a decline in film production, it is the oldest and one of the largest hubs of film and television production.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-LAFilmProductionDeclining-21) It has [one of the busiest container ports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_of_Los_Angeles "Port of Los Angeles") in the Americas.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-22)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-23)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-24) Despite an exodus of commerce and an [increasingly unreliable water supply](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_scarcity "Water scarcity"), Downtown Los Angeles is evolving as a cultural center with the world's largest showcase of architecture designed by [Frank Gehry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry "Frank Gehry").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-DowntownLosAngelesHurting-25) In 2024, the [Los Angeles metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Los_Angeles "Greater Los Angeles") had a [gross metropolitan product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_metropolitan_product "Gross metropolitan product") of over $1.295 trillion,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-fred-26) making it the city with the [third-largest GDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_by_GDP "List of cities by GDP") in the world, after [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_metropolitan_area "New York metropolitan area") and [Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_metropolitan_area "Tokyo metropolitan area"). Los Angeles hosted the [Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Olympics "Summer Olympics") in [1932](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1932_Summer_Olympics "1932 Summer Olympics") and [1984](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Summer_Olympics "1984 Summer Olympics"), and will host the games for a third time in [2028](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2028_Summer_Olympics "2028 Summer Olympics").

## Toponymy

See also: [Etymology of place names in Los Angeles County, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etymology_of_place_names_in_Los_Angeles_County,_California "Etymology of place names in Los Angeles County, California")

On September 4, 1781, a group of 44 settlers known as "[Los Pobladores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Pobladores "Los Angeles Pobladores")" founded the pueblo (town) they called [El Pueblo de Nuestra Señora la Reina de los Ángeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Pueblo_de_Nuestra_Se%C3%B1ora_la_Reina_de_los_%C3%81ngeles "El Pueblo de Nuestra Señora la Reina de los Ángeles"), 'The Town of [Our Lady the Queen of the Angels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Our_Lady_the_Queen_of_the_Angels?action=edit&redlink=1 "Our Lady the Queen of the Angels (page does not exist)")[[es](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgen%20de%20los%20%C3%81ngeles "es:Virgen de los Ángeles")]'.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-almanac-27) The original name of the settlement is disputed; the [Guinness Book of World Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinness_Book_of_World_Records "Guinness Book of World Records") rendered it as "El Pueblo de Nuestra Señora la Reina de los Ángeles del Río [Porciúncula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portiuncula "Portiuncula")"[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]; other sources have shortened or alternate versions of the longer name.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-28)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-29)

The local English pronunciation of the name of the city has varied over time. A 1953 article in the [journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Names_(journal) "Names (journal)") of the [American Name Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Name_Society "American Name Society") asserts that the pronunciation [/l ɔː s ˈ æ n dʒ əl ə s/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_lawss AN-jəl-əs_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key") was established following the 1850 incorporation of the city and that since the 1880s the pronunciation [/l oʊ s ˈ æ ŋ ɡ əl ə s/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_lohss ANG-gəl-əs_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key") emerged from a trend in California to give places Spanish (or Spanish-sounding) names and pronunciations.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-stein-30) In 1908, librarian [Charles Fletcher Lummis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Fletcher_Lummis "Charles Fletcher Lummis"), who argued for the name's pronunciation with a hard _g_ ([/ɡ/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")),[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-31)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-32) reported that there were at least 12 pronunciation variants.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-33) In the early 1900s, the _[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los\_Angeles\_Times "Los Angeles Times")_ advocated for pronouncing it _Loce AHNG-hayl-ais_ ([/l oʊ s ˈ ɑː ŋ h eɪ l eɪ s/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")), approximating Spanish [[los ˈaŋxeles]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish"), by printing the [respelling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Respelling "Respelling") under its masthead for several
