### Indigenous history

The settlement of [Indigenous Californians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_California "Indigenous peoples of California") in the modern [Los Angeles Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Basin "Los Angeles Basin") and the [San Fernando Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Fernando_Valley "San Fernando Valley") was dominated by the [Tongva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tongva "Tongva") (now also known as the _Gabrieleño_ since the era of Spanish colonization). The historic center of Tongva power in the region was the settlement of [Yaanga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yaanga "Yaanga") ([Tongva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tongva_language "Tongva language"): _Iyáangẚ_), meaning "place of the [poison oak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toxicodendron_diversilobum "Toxicodendron diversilobum")", which would eventually become the site where the Spanish founded the [Pueblo de Los Ángeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pueblo_de_Los_%C3%81ngeles "Pueblo de Los Ángeles"). _Iyáangẚ_ has also been translated as "the valley of smoke".[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-37)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-38)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-google86-39)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-sfgate2002-40)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-:02-19)

### Spanish rule

In 1542, maritime explorer [Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Rodr%C3%ADguez_Cabrillo "Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo") claimed the present-day area of southern California for the [Spanish Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire") during an official military expedition northward along the [Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean") coast from [New Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Spain "New Spain").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-41)[Gaspar de Portolà](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaspar_de_Portol%C3%A0 "Gaspar de Portolà") and [Franciscan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franciscan "Franciscan") missionary [Juan Crespí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Cresp%C3%AD "Juan Crespí") reached the present site of Los Angeles on August 2, 1769.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-42)

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Mission_San_Fernando_Rey_de_Espa%C3%B1a_%28Oriana_Day%29_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Mission_San_Fernando_Rey_de_Espa%C3%B1a_%28Oriana_Day%29_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mission_San_Fernando_Rey_de_Espa%C3%B1a_(Oriana_Day)_(cropped).jpg)

The [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Spain "Empire of Spain") founded [Mission San Fernando Rey de España](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_San_Fernando_Rey_de_Espa%C3%B1a "Mission San Fernando Rey de España") in 1797.

In 1771, Franciscan [friar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friar "Friar")[Junípero Serra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jun%C3%ADpero_Serra "Junípero Serra") directed the building of the [Mission San Gabriel Arcángel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_San_Gabriel_Arc%C3%A1ngel "Mission San Gabriel Arcángel"), the first [mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_(station) "Mission (station)") in the area.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-LeffingwellWorden2005-43) On September 4, 1781, a group of 44 settlers known as "[Los Pobladores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Pobladores "Los Angeles Pobladores")" founded the pueblo (town) they called [El Pueblo de Nuestra Señora la Reina de los Ángeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Pueblo_de_Nuestra_Se%C3%B1ora_la_Reina_de_los_%C3%81ngeles "El Pueblo de Nuestra Señora la Reina de los Ángeles"), 'The Town of Our Lady the Queen of the Angels'.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-almanac-27) The present-day city has the largest [Roman Catholic archdiocese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archdiocese_of_Los_Angeles "Archdiocese of Los Angeles") in the United States. Two-thirds of the Mexican or ([New Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Spain "New Spain")) settlers were [mestizo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mestizo "Mestizo") or [mulatto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mulatto "Mulatto"), a mixture of African, indigenous, and European ancestry.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-44) There was even one Asian Filipino from [Manila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila "Manila") (Antonio Miranda Rodríguez) who was reassigned to nearby Santa Barbara which was a fortress that needed his gun-smithing skills more.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-45) The settlement remained a small ranch town for decades, but by 1820, the population had increased to about 650 residents.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-46) Today, the pueblo is commemorated in the historic district of [Los Angeles Pueblo Plaza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Pueblo_de_Los_%C3%81ngeles_Historical_Monument "El Pueblo de Los Ángeles Historical Monument") and [Olvera Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olvera_Street "Olvera Street"), the oldest part of Los Angeles.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-Estrada2006-47)

### Mexican rule

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Portrait_of_Pio_Pico_%28Californian_State_Library%29_%28detail%29.jpg/250px-Portrait_of_Pio_Pico_%28Californian_State_Library%29_%28detail%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Portrait_of_Pio_Pico_(Californian_State_Library)_(detail).jpg)

[Californio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Californio "Californio") statesman [Pío Pico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Pico "Pío Pico"), who served as the last [Mexican governor of California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_governors_of_California_before_1850 "List of governors of California before 1850"), played an influential role in the development of Los Angeles in the late Mexican and early American eras.

[New Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Spain "New Spain") achieved its independence from the Spanish Empire in 1821, after which the pueblo existed within the [Mexican Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Mexican_Republic "First Mexican Republic"). During Mexican rule, Governor [Pío Pico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%ADo_Pico "Pío Pico") made Los Angeles the regional capital of [Alta California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alta_California "Alta California").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-48) By this time, the new republic introduced more [secularization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican_secularization_act_of_1833 "Mexican secularization act of 1833") acts within the Los Angeles region.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-49) In 1846, during the [Mexican–American War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican%E2%80%93American_War "Mexican–American War"), marines from the United States occupied the pueblo. This resulted in the [siege of Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Los_Angeles "Siege of Los Angeles"), where 150 Mexican militias fought the occupiers, who eventually surrendered.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-50)

Mexican rule ended following the American [Conquest of California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_California "Conquest of California"), part of the larger Mexican-American War. Americans took control from the [Californios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Californios "Californios") after a series of battles, culminating with the signing of the [Treaty of Cahuenga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Cahuenga "Treaty of Cahuenga") on January 13, 1847.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-51) The [Mexican Cession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican_Cession "Mexican Cession") was formalized in the [Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Guadalupe_Hidalgo "Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo") in 1848, which ceded Los Angeles and the rest of Alta California to the United States.

### Post-Conquest era

See also: [Victorian Downtown Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_Downtown_Los_Angeles "Victorian Downtown Los Angeles") and [Los Angeles in the 1920s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_in_the_1920s "Los Angeles in the 1920s")

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Treaty_of_Cahuenga.jpg/330px-Treaty_of_Cahuenga.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Treaty_of_Cahuenga.jpg)

The [Treaty of Cahuenga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Cahuenga "Treaty of Cahuenga"), signed in 1847 by Californio [Andrés Pico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9s_Pico "Andrés Pico") and American [John C. Frémont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_C._Fr%C3%A9mont "John C. Frémont"), ended the U.S. [Conquest of California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_California "Conquest of California").

[Railroads arrived](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Los_Angeles#Railroads "History of Los Angeles") with the completion of the [Southern Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Pacific_Railroad "Southern Pacific Railroad") line from [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco") to Los Angeles in 1876 and the [Santa Fe Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atchison,_Topeka_and_Santa_Fe_Railway "Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway") in 1885.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-Mulholland2002-52) Petroleum was discovered in the city and surrounding area in 1892, and by 1923, the discoveries helped [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California") become the country's largest oil producer, accounting for about one-quarter of the world's petroleum output.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-Kipen2011-53)

By 1900, the population had grown to more than 102,000,[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-54) putting pressure on the city's [water supply](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_supply "Water supply").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-55) The completion of the [Los Angeles Aqueduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Aqueduct "Los Angeles Aqueduct") in 1913, under the supervision of [William Mulholland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Mulholland "William Mulholland"), ensured the continued growth of the city.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-Reisner1993-56) Because of clauses in the city's charter that prevented the City of Los Angeles from selling or providing water from the aqueduct to any area outside its borders, many adjacent cities and communities felt compelled to join Los Angeles.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-LAgrowth-57)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-58)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-FinalReport-59)

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/Paramount_Pictures_studio_gate%2C_c._1940_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Paramount_Pictures_studio_gate%2C_c._1940_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Paramount_Pictures_studio_gate,_c._1940_(cropped).jpg)

In the early 20th century, [Hollywood studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_film_studios "Major film studios"), like [Paramount Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_Pictures "Paramount Pictures"), helped transform [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood,_Los_Angeles "Hollywood, Los Angeles") into the world capital of film and helped solidify LA as a global economic hub.

Los Angeles created the first municipal [zoning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoning "Zoning") ordinance in the United States. On September 14, 1908, the [Los Angeles City Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_City_Council,_1889%E2%80%931909 "Los Angeles City Council, 1889–1909") promulgated residential and industrial land use zones. The new ordinance established three residential zones of a single type, where industrial uses were prohibited. The proscriptions included barns, lumber yards, and any industrial land use employing machine-powered equipment. These laws were enforced against industrial properties after the fact. These prohibitions were in addition to existing activities that were already regulated as nuisances. These included explosives warehousing, gas works, oil drilling, slaughterhouses, and [tanneries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tannery "Tannery"). Although the council designated seven industrial zones, exemptions granted between 1908 and 1915 permitted industrial development within designated residential areas. There are two differences between the 1908 Residence District Ordinance and later zoning laws in the United States. First, the 1908 laws did not establish a comprehensive zoning map as the [1916 New York City Zoning Ordinance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoning_in_the_United_States#Origins_and_history "Zoning in the United States") did. Second, the residential zones did not distinguish types of housing; they treated apartments, hotels, and detached single-family housing equally.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-weiss80-60)

In 1910, Hollywood merged into Los Angeles, with 10 movie companies already operating in the city at the time. By 1921, more than 80 percent of the world's film industry was concentrated in L.A.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-Buntin2010-61) The money generated by the industry kept the city insulated from much of the economic loss suffered by the rest of the country during the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression_in_the_United_States "Great Depression in the United States").[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-YoungYoung2007-62) By 1930, the population surpassed one million.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-63) In 1932, the city hosted the [Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1932_Summer_Olympics "1932 Summer Olympics").

### Post–World War II

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/WSA_Photo_4235.jpg/250px-WSA_Photo_4235.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:WSA_Photo_4235.jpg)

The [California Shipbuilding Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Shipbuilding_Corporation "California Shipbuilding Corporation") on [Terminal Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminal_Island "Terminal Island") was among the many builders that made the [Port of Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_of_Los_Angeles "Port of Los Angeles") one of the country's largest [shipyards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shipyard "Shipyard") during World War II.

During the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_home_front_during_World_War_II "United States home front during World War II"), Los Angeles became a major center of wartime manufacturing, such as shipbuilding and aircraft. [Calship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Shipbuilding_Corporation "California Shipbuilding Corporation") built hundreds of [Liberty Ships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty_Ship "Liberty Ship") and [Victory Ships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_Ship "Victory Ship") on Terminal Island, and the Los Angeles area was the headquarters of six of the country's major aircraft manufacturers ([Douglas Aircraft Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Aircraft_Company "Douglas Aircraft Company"), [Hughes Aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hughes_Aircraft_Company "Hughes Aircraft Company"), [Lockheed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Corporation "Lockheed Corporation"), [North American Aviation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_Aviation "North American Aviation"), [Northrop Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northrop_Corporation "Northrop Corporation"), and [Vultee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vultee_Aircraft "Vultee Aircraft")). During the war, more aircraft were produced in one year than in all the pre-war years since the Wright brothers flew their first airplane in 1903, combined. Manufacturing in Los Angeles skyrocketed, and as [William S. Knudsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_S._Knudsen "William S. Knudsen"), of the National Defense Advisory Commission, put it, "We won because we smothered the enemy in an avalanche of production, the like of which he had never seen, nor dreamed possible."[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-64)

Following [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), a major influx of new residents and the expansion of defense and aerospace industries accelerated Los Angeles' urbanization. The resulting metropolitan growth caused the city to expand rapidly, [sprawling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_sprawl "Urban sprawl") northwest into the [San Fernando Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Fernando_Valley "San Fernando Valley").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-Bruegmann2006-65) The expansion of the state owned [Interstate Highway System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_Highway_System "Interstate Highway System") during the 1950s and 1960s helped propel suburban growth and signaled the demise of the city's privately owned [electrified rail system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Electric "Pacific Electric"), once the world's largest.

As a consequence of World War II, suburban growth, and population density, many amusement parks were built and operated in this area.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-Braun-66) An example is [Beverly Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Park_(amusement_park) "Beverly Park (amusement park)"), which was located at the corner of Beverly Boulevard and La Cienega before being closed and replaced by the [Beverly Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Center "Beverly Center").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-Jennings-67)

In the late 20th century, Los Angeles substantially reduced the amount of housing that could be built by drastically [downzoning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoning_in_the_United_States "Zoning in the United States") the city. In 1960, the city had a total zoned capacity for approximately 10 million people. By 1990, that capacity had fallen to 4.5 million as a result of policy decisions to ban housing through zoning.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-68)

Racial tensions led to the [Watts riots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watts_riots "Watts riots") in 1965, resulting in 34 deaths and over 1,000 injuries.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-Hinton2-69)

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/Olympic_Torch_Tower_of_the_Los_Angeles_Coliseum.jpg/250px-Olympic_Torch_Tower_of_the_Los_Angeles_Coliseum.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Olympic_Torch_Tower_of_the_Los_Angeles_Coliseum.jpg)

Opening ceremony of the [1984 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Summer_Olympics "1984 Summer Olympics") at the [LA Coliseum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Memorial_Coliseum "Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum")

In 1969, California became the birthplace of the Internet, as the first [ARPANET](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARPANET "ARPANET") transmission was sent from the [University of California, Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Los_Angeles "University of California, Los Angeles") (UCLA) to the [Stanford Research Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Research_Institute "Stanford Research Institute") in [Menlo Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menlo_Park,_California "Menlo Park, California").[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-HafnerLyon1999-70)

In 1973, [Tom Bradley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Bradley_(American_politician) "Tom Bradley (American politician)") was elected as the city's first African American mayor, serving for five terms until retiring in 1993. Other events in the city during the 1970s included the [Symbionese Liberation Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symbionese_Liberation_Army "Symbionese Liberation Army")'s [South Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Los_Angeles "South Los Angeles") standoff in 1974 and the [Hillside Stranglers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillside_Stranglers "Hillside Stranglers") murder cases in 1977–1978.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-vronsky187-71)

In early 1984, the city surpassed Chicago in population to become the second-largest city in the United States.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-72)

In 1984, the city hosted the Summer Olympic Games [for the second time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Summer_Olympics "1984 Summer Olympics"). Despite being [boycotted by 14 Communist countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Summer_Olympics_boycott "1984 Summer Olympics boycott"), the 1984 Olympics became more financially successful than any previous,[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-73) and the second Olympics to turn a profit; the other, according to an analysis of contemporary newspaper reports, was the [1932 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1932_Summer_Olympics "1932 Summer Olympics"), also held in Los Angeles.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-Zarnowski-74)

[![Image 28](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/02/48_California_Willshire_Grand_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-48_California_Willshire_Grand_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:48_California_Willshire_Grand_(cropped).jpg)

[Wilshire Grand Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilshire_Grand_Center "Wilshire Grand Center"), built in 2017, is the [tallest building in California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tallest_buildings_in_California "List of tallest buildings in California") and in the [Western United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_United_States "Western United States").

Racial tensions erupted on April 29, 1992, with the acquittal by a [Simi Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simi_Valley "Simi Valley") jury of four [Los Angeles Police Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Police_Department "Los Angeles Police Department") (LAPD) officers captured on videotape beating [Rodney King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodney_King "Rodney King"), culminating in [large-scale riots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_riots_of_1992 "Los Angeles riots of 1992").[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-RuckerUpton2007-75)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-76)

In 1994, the magnitude 6.7 [Northridge earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northridge_earthquake "Northridge earthquake") shook the city, causing $12.5 billion in damage and 72 deaths.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-77) The century ended with the [Rampart scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rampart_scandal "Rampart scandal"), one of the most extensive documented cases of police misconduct in American history.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-78)

### 21st century

In 2002, Mayor [James Hahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hahn "James Hahn") led the campaign against secession, resulting in voters defeating efforts by the San Fernando Valley and Hollywood to secede from the city.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-79)

In [2022](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Los_Angeles_mayoral_election "2022 Los Angeles mayoral election"), [Karen Bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karen_Bass "Karen Bass") became the city's first female [mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Los_Angeles "Mayor of Los Angeles"), making Los Angeles the largest U.S. city to have ever had a woman as mayor.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-80)

In January 2025, a series of [devastating wildfires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_2025_Southern_California_wildfires "January 2025 Southern California wildfires") caused by severe winds swept through Southern California, with the [Pacific Palisades fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palisades_Fire "Palisades Fire") causing widespread destruction in Los Angeles's northwestern community of [Pacific Palisades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Palisades,_Los_Angeles "Pacific Palisades, Los Angeles"), with many calling it the most destructive in the history of the city of Los Angeles.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-81)

In June 2025, the city experienced [protests and riots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/June_2025_Los_Angeles_protests "June 2025 Los Angeles protests") following raids by [United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Immigration_and_Customs_Enforcement "United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement") (ICE).[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-82) The Trump administration has targeted Los Angeles over its sanctuary city status, [sending in hundreds of federal agents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_deployment_of_federal_forces_in_the_United_States "2025 deployment of federal forces in the United States") to apprehend undocumented immigrants.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-83) Trump also dispatched the Army National Guard and US Marines without the consent of local governments.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-84)

Los Angeles will host the [2028 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2028_Summer_Olympics "2028 Summer Olympics") and [Paralympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2028_Summer_Paralympics "2028 Summer Paralympics"), making Los Angeles the third city to host the Olympics three times, after [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") and [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris").[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-85)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-86)

## Geography

### Topography

[![Image 29](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Los_Angeles_by_Sentinel-2%2C_2019-03-30.jpg/250px-Los_Angeles_by_Sentinel-2%2C_2019-03-30.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Los_Angeles_by_Sentinel-2,_2019-03-30.jpg)

Satellite view of Los Angeles

The city of Los Angeles covers a total area of 502.7 square miles (1,302 km 2), comprising 468.7 square miles (1,214 km 2) of land and 34.0 square miles (88 km 2) of water.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-gazetteer-87) The city extends for 44 miles (71 km) from north to south and for 29 miles (47 km) from east to west. The perimeter of the city is 342 miles (550 km).

Los Angeles is both flat and hilly. The highest point in the city proper is [Mount Lukens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Lukens "Mount Lukens") at 5,074 ft (1,547 m),[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-88)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-89) located in the foothills of the [San Gabriel Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Gabriel_Mountains "San Gabriel Mountains") at the north extent of the [Crescenta Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crescenta_Valley "Crescenta Valley"). The eastern end of the [Santa Monica Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Monica_Mountains "Santa Monica Mountains") stretches from [Downtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Los_Angeles "Downtown Los Angeles") to the Pacific Ocean and separates the Los Angeles Basin from the San Fernando Valley. Other hilly parts of Los Angeles include the [Mt. Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Washington,_Los_Angeles "Mt. Washington, Los Angeles") area north of Downtown, eastern parts such as [Boyle Heights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyle_Heights "Boyle Heights"), the [Crenshaw district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crenshaw,_Los_Angeles "Crenshaw, Los Angeles") around the [Baldwin Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baldwin_Hills,_Los_Angeles "Baldwin Hills, Los Angeles"), and the [San Pedro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Pedro,_Los_Angeles "San Pedro, Los Angeles") district.

Surrounding the city are much higher mountains. Immediately to the north lie the [San Gabriel Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Gabriel_Mountains "San Gabriel Mountains"), a popular recreation area for Angelenos. Its high point is [Mount San Antonio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_San_Antonio "Mount San Antonio"), locally known as Mount Baldy, which reaches 10,064 feet (3,068 m). Further afield, the highest point in southern California is [San Gorgonio Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Gorgonio_Mountain "San Gorgonio Mountain"), 81 miles (130 km) east of downtown Los Angeles,[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-90) with a height of 11,503 feet (3,506 m).

The [Los Angeles River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_River "Los Angeles River"), which is largely seasonal, is the primary [drainage channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drainage_channel "Drainage channel"). It was straightened and lined in 51 miles (82 km) of concrete by the [Army Corps of Engineers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Corps_of_Engineers "United States Army Corps of Engineers") to act as a flood control channel.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-Gumprecht2001-91) The river begins in the [Canoga Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canoga_Park,_Los_Angeles "Canoga Park, Los Angeles") district of the city, flows east from the San Fernando Valley along the north edge of the Santa Monica Mountains, and turns south through the city center, flowing to its mouth in the Port of [Long Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Beach,_California "Long Beach, California") at the Pacific Ocean. The smaller [Ballona Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballona_Creek "Ballona Creek") flows into the [Santa Monica Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Monica_Bay "Santa Monica Bay") at [Playa del Rey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playa_del_Rey,_Los_Angeles "Playa del Rey, Los Angeles").

Los Angeles is rich in native plant species partly because of its diversity of habitats, including beaches, [wetlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wetland "Wetland"), and mountains. The most prevalent plant communities are [coastal sage scrub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coastal_sage_scrub "Coastal sage scrub"), [chaparral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaparral "Chaparral") shrubland, and [riparian woodland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riparian_woodland "Riparian woodland").[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-Miller2008-92) Native plants include the [California poppy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_poppy "California poppy"), [matilija poppy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matilija_poppy "Matilija poppy"), [toyon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heteromeles "Heteromeles"), [ceanothus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceanothus "Ceanothus"), [chamise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chamise "Chamise"), [coast live oak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coast_live_oak "Coast live oak"), [sycamore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platanus_racemosa "Platanus racemosa"), [willow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willow "Willow") and [giant wildrye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leymus_condensatus "Leymus condensatus"). Many of these native species, such as the [Los Angeles sunflower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helianthus_nuttallii "Helianthus nuttallii"), have become so rare as to be considered endangered. [Mexican fan palms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washingtonia_filifera_var._robusta "Washingtonia filifera var. robusta"), [Canary Island palms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_canariensis "Phoenix canariensis"), [queen palms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syagrus_romanzoffiana "Syagrus romanzoffiana"), [date palms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Date_palm "Date palm"), and [California fan palms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washingtonia_filifera "Washingtonia filifera") are common in the Los Angeles area, although only the last is native to California, though still not native to the City of Los Angeles.

Los Angeles has several official flora:

*   The official flower is the bird of paradise (_[Strelitzia reginae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strelitzia\_reginae "Strelitzia reginae")_).[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-Communications2003-94)
*   The official plant is toyon (_[Heteromeles arbutifolia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heteromeles "Heteromeles")_).[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-95)

### Geology

[![Image 31](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/Mt._Lukens_overlooking_La_Crescenta-Montrose.jpg/250px-Mt._Lukens_overlooking_La_Crescenta-Montrose.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mt._Lukens_overlooking_La_Crescenta-Montrose.jpg)

[Mount Lukens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Lukens "Mount Lukens"), in the [San Gabriel Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Gabriel_Mountains "San Gabriel Mountains"), is the highest point in LA.

Los Angeles is subject to earthquakes because of its location on the [Pacific Ring of Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Fire "Ring of Fire"). The geologic instability has produced numerous [faults](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fault_(geology) "Fault (geology)"), which cause approximately 10,000 earthquakes annually in Southern California, though most of them are too small to be felt.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-quakes-100) The [strike-slip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strike-slip_fault "Strike-slip fault")[San Andreas Fault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Andreas_Fault "San Andreas Fault") system, which sits at the boundary between the [Pacific Plate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Plate "Pacific Plate") and the [North American Plate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_Plate "North American Plate"), passes through the Los Angeles metropolitan area. The segment of the fault passing through Southern California experiences a major earthquake roughly every 110 to 140 years, and [seismologists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seismologist "Seismologist") have warned about the next "big one", as the last major earthquake was the [1857 Fort Tejon earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1857_Fort_Tejon_earthquake "1857 Fort Tejon earthquake").[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-101) The Los Angeles basin and metropolitan area are also at risk from [blind thrust earthquakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_thrust_earthquake "Blind thrust earthquake").[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-102) Major earthquakes that have hit the Los Angeles area include the [1933 Long Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1933_Long_Beach_earthquake "1933 Long Beach earthquake"), [1971 San Fernando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1971_San_Fernando_earthquake "1971 San Fernando earthquake"), [1987 Whittier Narrows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_Whittier_Narrows_earthquake "1987 Whittier Narrows earthquake"), and the [1994 Northridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_Northridge_earthquake "1994 Northridge earthquake") events. All but a few are of low intensity and are not felt. The USGS has released the [UCERF California earthquake forecast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_earthquake_forecast "California earthquake forecast"), which models earthquake occurrence in California. Parts of the city are also vulnerable to [tsunamis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsunami "Tsunami"); harbor areas were damaged by waves from [Aleutian Islands earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1946_Aleutian_Islands_earthquake "1946 Aleutian Islands earthquake") in 1946, [Valdivia earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1960_Valdivia_earthquake "1960 Valdivia earthquake") in 1960, [Alaska earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_Alaska_earthquake "1964 Alaska earthquake") in 1964, [Chile earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Chile_earthquake "2010 Chile earthquake") in 2010 and [Japan earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_T%C5%8Dhoku_earthquake_and_tsunami "2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami") in 2011.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-103)

The city is divided into many different districts and neighborhoods,[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-104)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-105) some of which had been separately incorporated cities that eventually merged with Los Angeles.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-Abu-Lughod1999-106) These neighborhoods were developed piecemeal, and are well-defined enough that the city has signage which marks nearly all of them.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-107)

#### Overview

[![Image 32](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/The_Griffith_Observatory_at_night%2C_Mt._Hollywood%2C_Los_Angeles%2C_California%2C_U.S.jpg/250px-The_Griffith_Observatory_at_night%2C_Mt._Hollywood%2C_Los_Angeles%2C_California%2C_U.S.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Griffith_Observatory_at_night,_Mt._Hollywood,_Los_Angeles,_California,_U.S.jpg)

View of the [downtown Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Los_Angeles "Downtown Los Angeles") skyline from [Griffith Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Griffith_Park "Griffith Park")

The city's street patterns generally follow a [grid plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grid_plan "Grid plan"), with uniform block lengths and occasional roads that cut across blocks. However, this is complicated by rugged terrain, which has necessitated having different grids for each of the valleys that Los Angeles covers. Major streets are designed to move large volumes of traffic through many parts of the city, many of which are extremely long; [Sepulveda Boulevard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sepulveda_Boulevard "Sepulveda Boulevard") is 43 miles (69 km) long, while [Foothill Boulevard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foothill_Boulevard_(Southern_California) "Foothill Boulevard (Southern California)") is over 60 miles (97 km) long, reaching as far east as San Bernardino. Drivers in Los Angeles suffer from one of the worst rush hour periods in the world, according to an annual traffic index by navigation system maker, [TomTom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TomTom "TomTom"). LA drivers spend an additional 92 hours in traffic each year. During the peak rush hour, there is 80% congestion, according to the index.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles#cite_note-108)

Los Angeles is often characterized by the presence of [low-rise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-rise "Low-rise") buildings, in contrast to New York City. Outside of a few centers such as [downtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Los_Angeles "Downtown Los Angeles"), [Warner Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Center "Warner Center"), [Century City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Century_City "Century City"), [Koreatown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koreatown,_Los_Angeles "Koreatown, Los Angeles"), [Miracle Mile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miracle_Mile,_Los_Angeles "Miracle Mile, Los Angeles"), [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood,_Los_Angeles "Hollywood, Los Angeles"), and [Westwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westwood,_Los_Angeles "Westwood, Los Angeles"), skyscrapers and high-rise buildings are not common in Los Angeles. However, downtown Los Angeles alone has many buildings over 30 stories, with fourteen over 50 stories, and two over 70 stories, the tallest of which is the [Wilshire Grand Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilshire_Grand_Center "Wilshire Grand Center").

**Houston** ([/ˈ h juː s t ən/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/7/71/En-us-Houston.ogg/En-us-Houston.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:En-us-Houston.ogg "File:En-us-Houston.ogg")[_HEW-stən_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")) is the [most populous city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_in_Texas_by_population "List of cities in Texas by population") in the U.S. state of [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas") and the [Southern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_United_States "Southern United States"). It is the [fourth-most populous city in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_cities_by_population "List of United States cities by population"), with a population of 2.3 million at the [2020 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census"). The [Greater Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Houston "Greater Houston") metropolitan area, at 7.8 million residents, is the [fifth-most populous metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_statistical_area "Metropolitan statistical area") in the nation and [second-most populous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Texas_metropolitan_areas "List of Texas metropolitan areas") in Texas. Located in [Southeast Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Texas "Southeast Texas") near [Galveston Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galveston_Bay "Galveston Bay") and the [Gulf of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico"), Houston is the [county seat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_seat "County seat") of [Harris County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harris_County,_Texas "Harris County, Texas"). Covering a total area of 640.4 square miles (1,659 km 2),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-:16-8) it is the [ninth largest city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_cities_by_area "List of United States cities by area") in the country and the largest whose municipal government is not consolidated with a county, parish, or borough. Although primarily located within [Harris County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harris_County,_Texas "Harris County, Texas"), portions of the city extend into [Fort Bend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Bend_County,_Texas "Fort Bend County, Texas") and [Montgomery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery_County,_Texas "Montgomery County, Texas") counties. Houston also functions as the southeastern anchor of the [Texas Triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Triangle "Texas Triangle") megaregion.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-9)

Houston was founded by land investors on August 30, 1836,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-10) at the confluence of [Buffalo Bayou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo_Bayou "Buffalo Bayou") and [White Oak Bayou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Oak_Bayou "White Oak Bayou") (a point now known as [Allen's Landing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allen's_Landing "Allen's Landing")) and incorporated as a city on June 5, 1837.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-Allen's_Landing-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-HouHTO-12) The city is named after former General [Sam Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Houston "Sam Houston"), who was president of the [Republic of Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Texas "Republic of Texas") and had won [Texas's independence from Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Revolution "Texas Revolution") at the [Battle of San Jacinto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_San_Jacinto "Battle of San Jacinto")25 miles (40 km) east of Allen's Landing.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-HouHTO-12) After briefly serving as the [capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_city "Capital city") of the Texas Republic in the late 1830s, Houston grew steadily into a regional trading center for the remainder of the 19th century.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-:8-13) The 20th century brought a convergence of economic factors that fueled rapid growth in Houston, including a burgeoning port and railroad industry, the decline of [Galveston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galveston,_Texas "Galveston, Texas") as Texas's primary port following [a devastating 1900 hurricane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1900_Galveston_hurricane "1900 Galveston hurricane"), the subsequent construction of the [Houston Ship Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Ship_Channel "Houston Ship Channel"), and the [Texas oil boom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_oil_boom "Texas oil boom").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-:8-13) In the mid-20th century, Houston's economy diversified, as it became home to the [Texas Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Medical_Center "Texas Medical Center")—the world's largest concentration of healthcare and research institutions—and [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center"), home to the [Mission Control Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_C._Kraft_Jr._Mission_Control_Center "Christopher C. Kraft Jr. Mission Control Center").

Since the late 19th century, [Houston's economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Houston "Economy of Houston") has had a broad industrial base in [energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_in_Houston "Energy in Houston"), [manufacturing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manufacturing_in_Houston "Manufacturing in Houston"), aeronautics, and [transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Houston "Transportation in Houston"). Leading in healthcare sectors and building oilfield equipment, Houston has the second-most [_Fortune_ 500](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortune_500 "Fortune 500") headquarters of any U.S. municipality within its city limits.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-kearney-15) The [Port of Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_of_Houston "Port of Houston") ranks first in the United States in international waterborne tonnage handled and second in total cargo tonnage handled.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-port_ranking-16)

Nicknamed the "Bayou City", "Space City", "H-Town", and "the [713](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/713_area_code "713 area code")", Houston has become a [global city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_city "Global city"), with strengths in culture, medicine, and research. The city's population comprises various ethnic and religious backgrounds, as well as a large and growing international community. Houston is the [most diverse metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Houston "Demographics of Houston") in Texas and has been described as the most racially and ethnically diverse major city in the U.S.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-Hu-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-18) It is home to many cultural institutions and exhibits, such as the [Houston Museum District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Museum_District "Houston Museum District") and the [Houston Theater District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Theater_District "Houston Theater District").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-ikvngd-19)

## History

Main article: [History of Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Houston "History of Houston")

For a chronological guide, see [Timeline of Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Houston "Timeline of Houston").

Present-day Houston sits on land that was once occupied by the [Karankawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karankawa_people "Karankawa people") and the [Atakapa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atakapa "Atakapa") indigenous peoples for at least 2,000 years before the first known settlers arrived.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-22) These tribes are almost nonexistent today; this was most likely caused by foreign disease, and competition with various settler groups in the 18th and 19th centuries.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-23) However, the land then remained largely [uninhabited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uninhabited "Uninhabited") from the late 1700s until settlement in the 1830s.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-24)

### Early settlement to the 20th century

The Allen brothers—[Augustus Chapman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_Chapman_Allen "Augustus Chapman Allen") and [John Kirby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kirby_Allen "John Kirby Allen")—explored town sites on Buffalo Bayou and [Galveston Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galveston_Bay "Galveston Bay"). According to historian David McComb, "[T]he brothers, on August 26, 1836, bought from Elizabeth E. Parrott, wife of T.F.L. Parrott and widow of John Austin, the south half of the lower league [2,214-acre (896 ha) tract] granted to her by her late husband. They paid $5,000 total, but only $1,000 of this in cash; notes made up the remainder."[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-25)

The Allen brothers ran their first advertisement for Houston just four days later in the _Telegraph and Texas Register_, naming the notional town in honor of [Sam Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Houston "Sam Houston"), who would become [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Republic_of_Texas "President of the Republic of Texas") later that year.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-HouHTO-12) They successfully lobbied the [Republic of Texas Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_the_Republic_of_Texas "Congress of the Republic of Texas") to designate Houston as the temporary capital, agreeing to provide the new government with a state capitol building.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-tsha_AC-26) About a dozen persons resided in the town at the beginning of 1837, but that number grew to about 1,500 by the time the Texas Congress convened in Houston for the first time that May.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-HouHTO-12) The Republic of Texas granted Houston incorporation on June 5, 1837, as [James S. Holman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Sanders_Holman "James Sanders Holman") became its first mayor.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-HouHTO-12) In the same year, Houston became the county seat of Harrisburg County (now Harris County).[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-SHQa4-27)

In 1839, the Republic of Texas relocated its capital to [Austin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin,_Texas "Austin, Texas"). The town suffered another setback that year when a yellow fever epidemic claimed about one life for every eight residents, yet it persisted as a commercial center, forming a symbiosis with its Gulf Coast port, Galveston. Landlocked farmers brought their produce to Houston, using Buffalo Bayou to gain access to Galveston and the Gulf of Mexico. Houston merchants profited from selling staples to farmers and shipping the farmers' produce to Galveston.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-HouHTO-12)

The great majority of enslaved people in Texas came with their owners from the older slave states. Sizable numbers, however, came through the domestic slave trade. [New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans "New Orleans") was the center of this trade in the Deep South, but slave dealers were in Houston. Thousands of [enslaved](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_the_United_States "Slavery in the United States") black people lived near the city before the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"). Many of them near the city worked on sugar and cotton plantations,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-28) while most of those in the city limits had domestic and artisan jobs.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-29)

In 1840, the community established a chamber of commerce, in part to promote shipping and navigation at the newly created port on Buffalo Bayou.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-30)

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/Old_map-Houston-1873.jpg/250px-Old_map-Houston-1873.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Old_map-Houston-1873.jpg)

Houston, c.1873

By 1860, Houston had emerged as a commercial and [railroad hub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railroad "Railroad") for the export of cotton.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-SHQa4-27) Railroad spurs from the Texas inland converged in Houston, where they met rail lines to the ports of Galveston and [Beaumont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaumont,_Texas "Beaumont, Texas").

The [1860 U.S. Census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1860_United_States_census "1860 United States census") lists 4,845 inhabitants in Houston, including 1,069 [enslaved](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_the_United_States "Slavery in the United States")[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-31) (99% of the [city's African American population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_African_Americans_in_Houston "History of African Americans in Houston")).[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-Trevino29-32) During the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), Houston served as a headquarters for Confederate Major General [John B. Magruder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_B._Magruder "John B. Magruder"), who used the city as an organization point for the [Battle of Galveston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Galveston "Battle of Galveston").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-Sabine-33) After the Civil War, Houston businessmen initiated efforts to widen the city's extensive system of bayous so the city could accept more commerce between Downtown and the nearby port of Galveston. By 1890, Houston was the railroad center of Texas.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-34)

In 1900, after Galveston was struck by a devastating [hurricane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galveston_Hurricane_of_1900 "Galveston Hurricane of 1900"), efforts to make Houston into a viable deep-water port were accelerated.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-35) The following year, the discovery of [oil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petroleum "Petroleum") at the [Spindletop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spindletop "Spindletop")[oil field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_field "Oil field") near Beaumont prompted the development of the Texas petroleum industry.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-36) In 1902, President [Theodore Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt "Theodore Roosevelt") approved a $1 million improvement project for the Houston Ship Channel. By 1910, the city's population had reached 78,800, almost doubling from a decade before. African Americans formed a large part of the city's population, numbering 23,929 people, which was nearly one-third of Houston's residents.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-37)

President [Woodrow Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodrow_Wilson "Woodrow Wilson") opened the deep-water Port of Houston in 1914, seven years after digging began. By 1930, Houston had become Texas's most populous city and Harris County the most populous county.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-38) In 1940, the [U.S. Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau "United States Census Bureau") reported Houston's population as 77.5% White and 22.4% black.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-census1-39)

### World War II to the late 20th century

When [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_home_front_during_World_War_II "United States home front during World War II") started, tonnage levels at the port decreased and shipping activities were suspended; however, the war did provide economic benefits for the city. Petrochemical refineries and manufacturing plants were constructed along the ship channel because of the demand for petroleum and synthetic rubber products by the defense industry during the war.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-shipchannel-40)[Ellington Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellington_Airport_(Texas) "Ellington Airport (Texas)"), initially built during [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), was revitalized as an advanced training center for bombardiers and navigators.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-41) The [Brown Shipbuilding Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_Shipbuilding_Company "Brown Shipbuilding Company") was founded in 1942 to build ships for the [U.S. Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Navy "U.S. Navy") during World War II. Due to the boom in defense jobs, thousands of new workers migrated to the city, both black, and white people competing for the higher-paying jobs. President Roosevelt had established a policy of [nondiscrimination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-discrimination_law "Anti-discrimination law") for defense contractors, and black people gained some opportunities, especially in shipbuilding, although not without resistance from white people and increasing social tensions that erupted into occasional violence. Economic gains of black people who entered defense industries continued in the postwar years.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-42)

In 1945, the M.D. Anderson Foundation formed the [Texas Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Medical_Center "Texas Medical Center"). After the war, Houston's economy reverted to being primarily port-driven. In 1948, the city annexed several unincorporated areas, more than doubling its size. Houston proper began to spread across the region.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-HouHTO-12)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-43) In 1950, the availability of air conditioning provided impetus for many companies to relocate to Houston, where wages were lower than those in [the North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_United_States "Northern United States"); this resulted in an economic boom and produced a key shift in the city's economy toward the energy sector.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-45)

The increased production of the expanded shipbuilding industry during World War II spurred Houston's growth,[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-46) as did the establishment in 1961 of NASA's "Manned Spacecraft Center" (renamed the [Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson_Space_Center "Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center") in 1973). This was the stimulus for the development of the city's aerospace industry. The [Astrodome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astrodome "Astrodome"), nicknamed the "[Eighth Wonder of the World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eighth_Wonder_of_the_World "Eighth Wonder of the World")",[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-47) opened in 1965 as the world's first indoor domed sports stadium.

During the late 1970s, Houston had a population boom as people from the [Rust Belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust_Belt "Rust Belt") states moved to Texas in large numbers.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-48) The new residents came for numerous employment opportunities in the petroleum industry, created as a result of the [Arab oil embargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_oil_crisis "1973 oil crisis"). With the increase in professional jobs, Houston has become a destination for many college-educated persons, most recently including African Americans in a [reverse Great Migration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Great_Migration "New Great Migration") from northern areas.

In 1997, Houstonians elected [Lee P. Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_P._Brown "Lee P. Brown") as the city's first African American mayor.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-49)

### Early 21st century

Houston has continued to grow into the 21st century, with the population increasing 15.7% from 2000 to 2022.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-50)

Oil and gas have continued to fuel Houston's economic growth, with major oil companies including [Phillips 66](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phillips_66 "Phillips 66"), [ConocoPhillips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ConocoPhillips "ConocoPhillips"), [Occidental Petroleum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occidental_Petroleum "Occidental Petroleum"), [Halliburton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halliburton "Halliburton"), and [ExxonMobil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ExxonMobil "ExxonMobil") having their headquarters in the Houston area. In 2001, [Enron Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enron_Corporation "Enron Corporation"), a Houston company with $100 billion in revenue, became engulfed in an [accounting scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enron_scandal "Enron scandal") which bankrupted the company in 2001.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-51) Healthcare had also emerged as a major industry in Houston. The [Texas Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Medical_Center "Texas Medical Center") is now the largest medical complex in the world and employs over 120,000 people.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-52)

In the first decade of the 21st century, three new sports stadiums opened downtown. In 2000, the [Houston Astros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Astros "Houston Astros") opened their new baseball stadium, [Daikin Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daikin_Park "Daikin Park"), in downtown adjacent to the old [Union Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Station_(Houston) "Union Station (Houston)"). The [Houston Texans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Texans "Houston Texans") were formed in 2002 as an [NFL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFL "NFL") expansion team, replacing the [Houston Oilers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Oilers "Houston Oilers"), which had left the city in 1996. [Reliant Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reliant_Stadium "Reliant Stadium") opened the same year. In 2003, the [Toyota Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toyota_Center "Toyota Center") opened as the home for the [Houston Rockets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Rockets "Houston Rockets"). In 2005, the [Houston Dynamo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Dynamo "Houston Dynamo") soccer team was formed. In [2017](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_World_Series "2017 World Series"), the Houston Astros won their first [World Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Series "World Series").

#### Flooding and storms

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Harvey_flooding_%2836527844190%29.jpg/250px-Harvey_flooding_%2836527844190%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Harvey_flooding_(36527844190).jpg)

[Hurricane Harvey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Harvey "Hurricane Harvey") flooding

[Flooding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flooding "Flooding") has been a recurring problem in the Houston area. In June 2001, [Tropical Storm Allison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Allison "Tropical Storm Allison") dumped up to 40 inches (1,000 mm) of rain on parts of Houston, causing what was then the worst flooding in the city's history and billions of dollars in damage, and killed 20 people in Texas.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-53) In August 2005, Houston became a shelter to more than 150,000 people from New Orleans, who evacuated from [Hurricane Katrina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Katrina "Hurricane Katrina").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-54) One month later, about 2.5 million Houston-area residents evacuated when [Hurricane Rita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Rita "Hurricane Rita") approached the [Gulf Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Coast_of_the_United_States "Gulf Coast of the United States"), leaving little damage to the Houston area. This was the largest urban evacuation in the history of the United States.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-56)

In May 2015, seven people died after 12 inches of rain fell in 10 hours during what is known as the Memorial Day Flood. Eight people died in April 2016 during a storm that dropped 17 inches of rain.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-wild_west-57) The worst came in late August 2017, when [Hurricane Harvey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Harvey "Hurricane Harvey") stalled over southeastern Texas, much like Tropical Storm Allison did sixteen years earlier, causing severe flooding in the Houston area, with some areas receiving over 50 inches (1,300 mm) of rain.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-gallons-58) The rainfall exceeded 50 inches in several areas locally, breaking the national record for rainfall. The damage for the Houston area was estimated at up to $125 billion [U.S. dollars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._dollars "U.S. dollars"),[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-59) and was considered to be one of the worst [natural disasters in the history of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_natural_disasters_in_the_United_States "List of natural disasters in the United States"),[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-Hurricane_Harvey-60) with the death toll exceeding 70 people. Houston's lack of zoning laws allowed unregulated building of residential homes and other structures in flood-prone areas.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-auto3-61) However, it also resulted in more concentrated development in already urban areas than in wetlands and suburbs.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-62) Mayor Sylvester Turner tweeted of Hurricane Harvey that "zoning wouldn't have changed anything. We would have been a city with zoning that flooded."[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-63)

On May 16, 2024, a [strong derecho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Houston_derecho "2024 Houston derecho") caused widespread damage across the city and surrounding metropolitan area.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-65)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-66)

## Geography

Main article: [Geography of Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Houston "Geography of Houston")

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/40/Houston_by_Sentinel-2%2C_2020-09-30_%28small_version%29.jpg/250px-Houston_by_Sentinel-2%2C_2020-09-30_%28small_version%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Houston_by_Sentinel-2,_2020-09-30_(small_version).jpg)

Satellite image of Houston, 2020

Houston is 165 miles (266 km) east of [Austin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin,_Texas "Austin, Texas"),[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-67)88 miles (142 km) west of the [Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana "Louisiana") border,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-68) and 250 miles (400 km) south of [Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas "Dallas").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-69) The city has a total area of 637.4 square miles (1,651 km 2);[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-:16-8) this comprises over 599.59 square miles (1,552.9 km 2) of land and 22.3 square miles (58 km 2) covered by water.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-70) Most of Houston is on the [gulf coastal plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Gulf_coastal_grasslands "Western Gulf coastal grasslands"), and its vegetation is classified as [Western Gulf coastal grasslands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Gulf_coastal_grasslands "Western Gulf coastal grasslands") while further north, it transitions into a subtropical jungle, the [Big Thicket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Thicket "Big Thicket").

Much of the city was built on forested land, marshes, or swamps, and all are still visible in surrounding areas.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-71) Flat terrain and extensive greenfield development have combined to worsen flooding.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-72) Downtown stands about 50 feet (15 m) above sea level,[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-73) and the highest point in far northwest Houston is about 150 feet (46 m) in elevation.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-74) The city once relied on groundwater for its needs, but land [subsidence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subsidence "Subsidence") forced the city to turn to ground-level water sources such as [Lake Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Houston "Lake Houston"), [Lake Conroe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Conroe "Lake Conroe"), and [Lake Livingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Livingston "Lake Livingston").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-HouHTO-12)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-USGS_Subsidence_Fault_Creep-75) The city owns surface water rights for 1.20 billion U.S. gallons (4.5 Gl) of water a day in addition to 150 million U.S. gallons (570 Ml) a day of groundwater.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-76)

Houston has four major [bayous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayou "Bayou") passing through the city that accept water from the extensive drainage system. Buffalo Bayou runs through Downtown and the [Houston Ship Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Ship_Channel "Houston Ship Channel"), and has three tributaries: White Oak Bayou, which runs through the Houston Heights community northwest of Downtown and then towards Downtown; [Brays Bayou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brays_Bayou "Brays Bayou"), which runs along the Texas Medical Center;[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-77) and [Sims Bayou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sims_Bayou "Sims Bayou"), which runs through the south of Houston and Downtown Houston. The ship channel continues past Galveston and then into the Gulf of Mexico.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-shipchannel-40)

### Geology

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Houston_Texas_14Mar2018_SkySat.jpg/250px-Houston_Texas_14Mar2018_SkySat.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Houston_Texas_14Mar2018_SkySat.jpg)

Aerial view of central Houston, showing Downtown and surrounding neighborhoods, March 2018

Houston is a flat, [marshy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshy "Marshy") area where an extensive drainage system has been built. The adjoining prairie land drains into the city, which is prone to flooding.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-78) Underpinning Houston's land surface are [unconsolidated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consolidation_(geology) "Consolidation (geology)") clays, clay shales, and poorly cemented sands up to several miles deep. The region's geology developed from river deposits formed from the erosion of the [Rocky Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Mountains "Rocky Mountains"). These [sediments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sediment "Sediment") consist of a series of sands and clays deposited on decaying organic marine matter, that over time, transformed into oil and natural gas. Beneath the layers of sediment is a water-deposited layer of [halite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halite "Halite"), a rock salt. The porous layers were compressed over time and forced upward. As it pushed upward, the salt dragged surrounding sediments into [salt dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_dome "Salt dome") formations, often trapping oil and gas that seeped from the surrounding porous sands. The thick, rich, sometimes black, surface soil is suitable for rice farming in suburban outskirts where the city continues to grow.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-79)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-80)

The Houston area has over 150 active [faults](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fault_(geology) "Fault (geology)") (estimated to be 300 [active faults](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Active_fault "Active fault")) with an aggregate length of up to 310 miles (500 km),[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-81)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-82)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-83) including the [Long Point–Eureka Heights fault system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Point%E2%80%93Eureka_Heights_fault_system "Long Point–Eureka Heights fault system") which runs through the center of the city. Land in some areas southeast of Houston is sinking because water has been pumped out of the ground for many years. It may be associated with slip along the faults; however, the slippage is slow and not considered an earthquake, where stationary faults must slip suddenly enough to create seismic waves.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-84) These faults also tend to move at a smooth rate in what is termed "[fault creep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aseismic_creep "Aseismic creep")",[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston#cite_note-USGS_Subsidence_Fault_Creep-75) which further reduces the risk of an earthquake.
